lines: A hundred items, a capacity written in bits: this table fills in a blink, about a hundred thousand cells.
Append ten more bits to that same capacity and it is a hundred million. Thirty more, and it passes a hundred trillion.
Before the reveal, think about this: bin packing is NP-complete too, and it has numbers in it just like knapsack does.
answer: A table big enough to track every bin's load has one dimension per bin, so it grows exponentially with the bin count.
That has nothing to do with how the item sizes themselves are written down, so shrinking them buys nothing here.

lines: Asking whether some value can fit under a weight limit is NP-complete on paper. A table with one row per item answers it anyway, in one pass.
That table's size tracks the capacity's actual value, not the length of the number written down for it.
Ten bits gives about a hundred thousand cells, twenty gives about a hundred million, forty gives over a hundred trillion.
Write that capacity as a short string of bits, or as one tally mark for every single unit of value.
The table tracks the tally strip's length, not the bit string's. That is what pseudo-polynomial actually means.
A problem is weakly NP-hard when only its compact, binary encoding makes it hard, and some pseudo-polynomial algorithm may still exist.
Partition is the standard example: shrink its numbers and every hard instance simply disappears.
Running that dynamic program for real, one more bit at a time, its measured time roughly doubles with every bit appended.
That is exactly what a table with twice as many cells should cost, nothing more mysterious than that.
Before the reveal, think about this: three-partition is built so its hardest instances already have small numbers.
answer: There is no compact encoding to blame here, since the numbers were already small to begin with.
So shrinking them further removes nothing, and the problem stays exactly as hard as it was.

lines: A problem is strongly NP-hard when it stays NP-hard even with every number bounded by a polynomial in the input's length.
That is the same thing as staying hard when every number is written out in unary. Three-partition is the standard example.
A solver on three-partition instances with every number kept small still fans out sharply as more triples are added.
No single number in the instance ever grows, yet the search tree's size climbs fast anyway.
Suppose a strongly NP-hard problem had a pseudo-polynomial algorithm after all. Bounding its numbers would make that algorithm run in ordinary polynomial time.
But the problem is, by definition, still NP-hard on exactly those bounded instances. That is the whole contradiction.
Bin packing's hardness lives in the interaction of many bins with many different sizes, together.
Fix the number of bins and it becomes pseudo-polynomial. Fix the bin capacity instead and it becomes polynomial outright.
Strong NP-hardness rules out more than an exact algorithm: it also rules out a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme, unless P equals NP.
Knapsack's own such scheme, built on its weak hardness instead, belongs to a later topic on approximation.
Knapsack's table is polynomial in the value of its numbers, so shrinking those numbers shrinks the table away entirely.
Bin packing's hardness lives in how its bins interact, so no amount of shrinking the sizes ever shrinks that away.
